entries.sentence: The NHS lists hormonal, long-acting, barrier, emergency and permanent methods; they differ in how they work and how long they last.
entries.note: Groups and differences from NHS methods page.

entries.sentence: The NHS groups contraception into hormonal methods, coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options.
entries.note: Summarises groups.

entries.sentence: NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible methods that need no daily attention.
entries.note: NICE leaflet.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists only condoms and internal condoms as protecting against STIs, which the hormonal methods do not.
entries.note: STI list.

entries.sentence: Emergency contraception is the emergency pill or the copper IUD, each with a time limit after sex.
entries.note: Emergency options and time limits.

entries.sentence: The NHS says contraception is free, from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies.
entries.note: Free from the three places.

entries.sentence: The NHS contraception guide groups the methods it lists in several ways.
entries.note: NHS guide lists hormonal methods, coils, barrier methods, sterilisation and emergency contraception.

entries.sentence: These are hormonal methods, copper coils, barrier methods, emergency contraception and permanent options.
entries.note: Same list.

entries.sentence: The hormonal methods are the combined pill, the progestogen-only pill (or mini pill), the patch, the vaginal ring, the implant, the injection and the IUS, which is a hormonal coil.
entries.note: Combined pill has progestogen and oestrogen; mini pill progestogen only; patch and ring release both; implant, injection, IUS release progestogen.

entries.sentence: The IUD, or copper coil, contains no hormones.
entries.note: IUD inserted into womb, contains no hormones.

entries.sentence: The barrier methods are condoms, internal (female) condoms, the diaphragm and the cap.
entries.note: Barrier methods listed.

entries.sentence: Female sterilisation and vasectomy are the permanent methods.
entries.note: Both permanent.

entries.sentence: The NHS says contraception is free.
entries.note: Search summary: contraception is free on the NHS.

entries.sentence: The combined pill contains two hormones, progestogen and oestrogen.
entries.note: Combined pill contains progestogen and oestrogen.

entries.sentence: The patch and the vaginal ring release both of these hormones too.
entries.note: Patch and ring release both hormones.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the combined pill stops the ovaries releasing an egg each month.
entries.note: What is the combined pill? - NHS: stops ovaries releasing an egg each month.

entries.sentence: NHS inform Scotland adds that the hormones make it harder for sperm to reach an egg and thin the lining of the womb.
entries.note: NHS inform: hormones make it difficult for sperm to get to an egg and thin the womb lining.

entries.sentence: The patch is described as working in a similar way, and it also thickens the mucus at the neck of the womb.
entries.note: Patch stops release of an egg, thickens cervical mucus, thins womb lining; blended summary, page not isolated.

entries.sentence: The progestogen-only pill contains a man-made version of progestogen and, unlike the combined pill, no oestrogen.
entries.note: Contains artificial progestogen, no oestrogen.

entries.sentence: An NHS trust page says its main action is to thicken the mucus at the neck of the womb, which hinders sperm.
entries.note: Hope House NHS page: main action thickening cervical mucus.

entries.sentence: The injection contains progestogen, and its main action is to stop the ovaries releasing an egg.
entries.note: Injection: progestogen, stops ovaries releasing egg as main action; blended.

entries.sentence: The pill, patch and ring are used regularly, while the injection is repeated every few weeks, depending on the type.
entries.note: Injections given every 8 to 13 weeks depending on type; wording kept to 'few weeks'.

entries.sentence: NICE calls the injection, IUD, IUS and implant long-acting reversible contraception.
entries.note: NICE public leaflet: injections, IUDs, IUS and implants are LARC.

entries.sentence: It says these methods, unlike the pill or condoms, do not need attention every day or at each sex act.
entries.note: NICE: do not need daily attention or attention at each sex act.

entries.sentence: They are called reversible because they can be stopped when someone decides to become pregnant.
entries.note: NICE: can stop using them if you want to get pregnant.

entries.sentence: The NHS says the copper coil lasts for years, and the length depends on the type.
entries.note: IUD: 5 or 10 years depending on type; kept to words.

entries.sentence: The hormonal coil and the implant also last for years, though sources give different lengths.
entries.note: IUS 3 or 6 years (NHS) vs 3 to 8 (NHS inform); implant 3 or 5 years in different sources.

entries.sentence: The injection works for a much shorter time, in weeks rather than years.
entries.note: Injection 8 to 13 weeks depending on type.

entries.sentence: Several NHS sexual health services say fertility returns soon after an implant, IUS or IUD is taken out.
entries.note: NHS-linked services say fertility returns immediately after removal; one leaflet cited.

entries.sentence: After the injection, fertility can take longer to return, with one NHS-linked source saying up to a year.
entries.note: Up to 12 months to return to normal levels, per one source.

entries.sentence: Barrier methods put a physical barrier between sperm and egg.
entries.note: Barrier methods provide a physical barrier preventing sperm and egg getting together.

entries.sentence: Examples include condoms, internal condoms, caps and diaphragms.
entries.note: Listed barrier methods.

entries.sentence: They are used at the time of sex, rather than daily or over years.
entries.note: Implied by NICE contrast of long-acting methods with 'each sex act'.

entries.sentence: Condoms help prevent pregnancy and sexually transmitted infections, or STIs.
entries.note: Condoms help prevent pregnancy and STIs.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists only condoms and internal condoms as methods that protect against STIs.
entries.note: Methods that protect against STIs: condoms, female condoms.

entries.sentence: The hormonal methods do not protect against STIs.
entries.note: Hormonal methods do not provide protection against STIs.

entries.sentence: Emergency contraception is used after sex to help prevent pregnancy.
entries.note: NHS emergency contraception page; emergency pill taken after sex.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists emergency pills and the copper IUD as the options.
entries.note: Emergency pill; IUD can be used as emergency contraception.

entries.sentence: There are two main emergency pills in the UK, and each works within a set time after sex.
entries.note: Levonorgestrel and ulipristal acetate each have a time limit.

entries.sentence: The NHS gives the limit as 3 days for one type of pill and 5 days for the other.
entries.note: Emergency pill taken within 3 or 5 days after sex, depending on the type.

entries.sentence: A copper IUD can also be fitted as emergency contraception, and one NHS source says this works within five days of unprotected sex.
entries.note: Copper IUD works within five days of unprotected sex.

entries.sentence: A nurse or doctor fits the IUD, usually at a sexual health clinic or GP surgery, after making an appointment.
entries.note: Appointment needed; fitted by nurse or doctor at clinic or GP surgery.

entries.sentence: Emergency contraception is also free from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies.
entries.note: Free emergency contraception from clinics, some GPs, some pharmacies.

entries.sentence: The NHS lists female sterilisation and vasectomy as permanent methods.
entries.note: Sterilisation lasts forever (it is permanent).

entries.sentence: It says sterilisation lasts forever.
entries.note: Same.

entries.sentence: In a vasectomy, the tube that carries sperm from the testicles to the penis is tied, cut or sealed.
entries.note: Search result describing vasectomy.

entries.sentence: A vasectomy is free on the NHS, although one source notes that waiting lists can be long.
entries.note: Vasectomy free on NHS though waiting lists can be very long.

entries.sentence: Information and advice about sterilisation is available from a GP surgery or a sexual health clinic.
entries.note: Advice from GP surgery or sexual health clinic.

entries.sentence: Contraception is free on the NHS.
entries.note: Contraception is free on the NHS.

entries.sentence: It is available from sexual health clinics, some GP surgeries and some pharmacies.
entries.note: Three main places.

entries.sentence: Sexual health clinics are also called family planning, GUM or contraception clinics.
entries.note: Alternative names for sexual health clinics.

entries.sentence: Under the NHS Pharmacy Contraception Service in England, a person does not need to be registered with a GP.
entries.note: No GP registration needed for the pharmacy service.

entries.sentence: Supplies of contraception and emergency contraception through this route are free and exempt from prescription charges.
entries.note: All supplies free, exempt from prescription charges.

entries.sentence: The NHS website lets people find GPs, sexual health clinics and pharmacies by postcode.
entries.note: Find by postcode.

entries.sentence: NHS inform Scotland and NHS 111 Wales publish their own contraception pages for those nations.
entries.note: NHS inform page and NHS 111 Wales page returned by search; only the existence of the pages is stated.
